Pertanto, il suo parere non poteva essere trascurato su nessun argomento; quando mi espresse le sue opinioni e le sue esperienze riguardo al [[concepts/spiritualism|spiritualismo]], fui inevitabilmente colpito, anche se la mia filosofia personale era troppo solida per essere facilmente influenzata. Ero troppo povero per assumere medium professionisti; lavorare su tali argomenti senza un medium è come praticare l’astronomia senza un telescopio. Una sola volta, un anziano con presunte capacità psichiche venne da noi in cambio di una piccola somma di denaro e ci fece una dimostrazione: entrò in uno stato di trance caratterizzato da respiri affannosi, per poi sottoporci tutti a dei test. Il mio risultato fu certamente molto significativo: la risposta che ricevette fu “Non leggere il libro di Leigh Hunt”. In quel momento esitavo se leggere o meno il suo “Comic Dramatists of the Restoration”, perché da un lato si trattava di letteratura, dall’altro il modo in cui era scritto mi repelleva. Questo fu quindi un test molto efficace riguardo alla telepatia, anche se non lo considererei una prova decisiva. Ero così colpito che ne scrissi per la rivista settimanale dedicata alle questioni psichiche “Light”; nel 1887, dunque, dichiarai pubblicamente di essere uno studioso di questi argomenti. Sono passati trentasette anni da allora, quindi ora sono davvero un “studente anziano”. Da quel momento in poi ho letto e riflettuto molto su queste questioni, anche se solo più tardi nella mia vita ho realizzato verso cosa tutto ciò stesse portando. Tratterò questo argomento in modo dettagliato in una sezione finale, così che coloro a cui interessa meno possano evitarla.
Ero profondamente interessato e attratto dalla Teosofia per un anno o due, perché mentre lo [[concepts/spiritualism|spiritualismo]] sembrava all’epoca rappresentare il caos in termini filosofici, la Teosofia presentava un quadro molto ben congegnato e razionale; alcune delle sue dottrine, in particolare quelle sulla reincarnazione e sul karma, sembravano offrire spiegazioni per alcune anomalie della vita. Lessi “Il mondo occulto” di Sinnett e, in seguito, con ancora maggiore ammirazione, la sua eccellente esposizione della Teosofia in “Buddismo esoterico”, un libro davvero notevole. Lo incontrai anche personalmente, poiché era un vecchio amico del generale Drayson, e fui colpito dalla sua conversazione. Tuttavia, poco dopo apparve il rapporto del dottor Hodgson sulle indagini condotte su Madame Blavatsky ad Adyar, che scosse profondamente la mia fiducia in lei. È vero che successivamente la signora Besant pubblicò una solida difesa della Teosofia, suggerendo che Hodgson potesse essere stato ingannato; tuttavia il libro “Una sacerdotessa di Iside”, che contiene molte delle sue stesse lettere, lascia un’impressione negativa, e anche le opere postume di Sinnett sembrano indicare che avesse perso fiducia nella Teosofia. D’altra parte, il colonnello Olcott dimostra che quella donna possedeva senza dubbio vere capacità psichiche, qualunque ne fosse la fonte. Per quanto riguarda lo spiritualismo, sembra che lei ne fosse interessata soltanto agli aspetti fenomenologici più superficiali; i suoi libri dimostrano un’eccezionale erudizione e capacità di lavoro, anche se spesso riproducono semplicemente le conclusioni altrui. Tuttavia sarebbe ingiusto condannare questa antica saggezza soltanto perché è stata diffusa da una persona così straordinaria e controversa. Nel nostro ambito dell’occultismo ci sono stati molti medium disonesti, ma li abbiamo smascherati non appena ne abbiamo avuto l’opportunità; la Teosofia, liberandosi completamente dall’influenza di Madame Blavatsky, sarà in una posizione molto più forte. In ogni caso, essa non avrebbe mai potuto soddisfare le mie esigenze, poiché richiedo prove concrete e solide; se dovessi tornare a una fede cieca, mi ritroverei nuovamente nel gruppo da cui ero “scappato”.  
La mia vita era piacevole: avevo successo letterario, un lavoro che mi occupava adeguatamente e uno sport di cui parlerò in un capitolo successivo. Tuttavia, improvvisamente, un evento straordinario scosse la mia routine quotidiana, causando un cambiamento radicale nella mia vita e nei miei piani. Ci era nata una figlia, Mary; la nostra famiglia era felice, e poiché non avevo ambizioni personali, dato che le cose semplici della vita mi piacevano molto, avrei potuto rimanere per sempre a Southsea, se non fosse stato per quell’episodio. Tutto iniziò nel 1890, quando Koch annunciò di aver scoperto una cura efficace per la tubercolosi e che l’avrebbe dimostrata in un certo giorno a Berlino.
All’improvviso provai un forte desiderio di andare a Berlino per assistere a ciò che stava per accadere. Non riuscivo a fornire alcuna spiegazione logica per questo impulso, ma era qualcosa di irresistibile e decisi immediatamente di partire. Se fossi stato un famoso medico o uno specialista in una determinata branca della medicina, la mia decisione avrebbe avuto più senso; tuttavia, in realtà non ero particolarmente interessato ai recenti sviluppi della mia professione e credevo fermamente che gran parte di ciò che veniva definito “progresso” fosse in realtà illusorio. Comunque, dopo aver preparato rapidamente le mie cose, partii da solo per questa strana avventura. Avevo scambiato alcune lettere con il signor W. T. Stead riguardo a una certa questione, e passando per Londra decisi di andare dal suo ufficio presso la “Review of Reviews” per chiedergli se poteva presentarmi al dottor Koch o al dottor Bergmann, che avrebbero tenuto le dimostrazioni. Il signor Stead fu molto gentile con questo sconosciuto medico provinciale e mi diede una lettera da consegnare all’Ambasciatore britannico, Sir Edward Malet, e al corrispondente del “Times”, il signor Lowe. Mi chiese anche di scrivere un breve ritratto del dottor Koch, aggiungendo che nel numero di quel mese avrebbe pubblicato un articolo sul conte Mattei e nel successivo uno su Koch. Risposi: “Allora avrete in sequenza l’uomo più grande della scienza europea e il più grande ciarlatano d’Europa”. Stead mi guardò con rabbia, poiché a quel tempo il trattamento di Mattei con l’elettricità blu era particolarmente di moda tra i suoi seguaci. Comunque, ci lasciammo in buoni rapporti e mantenemmo un contatto distaccato per tutta la vita, anche se in seguito ebbero delle forti divergenze di opinione durante la guerra boera. Era un uomo coraggioso e onesto; a volte era impulsivo, ma proprio questa sua impulsività lo rendeva una grande forza del bene. Per quanto riguarda le conoscenze psichiche, era davvero un passo avanti rispetto alla sua epoca, anche se il modo in cui le esprimeva a volte poteva risultare inappropriato. Quella notte partii per Berlino e mi ritrovai sul treno espresso diretto in Germania insieme a un bellissimo e cortese medico londinese che aveva lo stesso scopo del mio. Trascorremmo gran parte della notte a chiacchierare; scoprii che si chiamava Malcolm Morris e che anche lui era stato un medico provinciale, ma che poi era arrivato a Londra ed era diventato molto famoso come specialista in dermatologia a Harley Street. Quella fu l’inizio di una amicizia che è durata per molti anni.
Arrivato a Berlino, la cosa più importante era assistere alla dimostrazione di Bergmann, che avrebbe avuto luogo il giorno dopo alle dodici. Andai dal nostro ambasciatore, ma fui costretto ad aspettare a lungo; ricevetti un’accoglienza fredda e fui congedato senza alcun aiuto o conforto. Poi provai a contattare il corrispondente del “The Times”, ma nemmeno lui poté aiutarmi. Lui e sua moglie gentile mi mostrarono ogni sorta di cortesia e mi invitarono a cena quella sera, ma i biglietti semplicemente non erano disponibili; né denaro né insistenze riuscirono a ottenerne uno. Mi venne l’idea folle di cercare di procurarmi un biglietto direttamente da Koch e mi recai a casa sua. Lì ebbi la curiosa esperienza di vedere arrivare la sua posta: un grande sacco pieno di lettere, che vennero disposte sul pavimento dell’ingresso e mostravano ogni tipo di timbro esistente in Europa. Era un segno di tutte quelle vite distrutte e cuori stanchi che si rivolgevano a Berlino nella speranza di trovare una soluzione. Tuttavia, Koch rimase un profeta velato: non volle incontrare né me né nessun altro. Ero davvero al limite delle mie risorse e non riuscivo a immaginare come potessi raggiungere il mio scopo.  
Il giorno dopo andai nel grande edificio dove avrebbe dovuto tenersi la conferenza e, corrompendo il portiere, riuscii ad entrare nell’atrio esterno. Un enorme pubblico si stava radunando nella stanza successiva. Provai di nuovo a corrompere qualcuno per essere fatto entrare, ma l’ufficiale divenne aggressivo. La gente passava davanti a me, ma io rimanevo sempre all’ingresso. Alla fine tutti erano entrati, quando improvvisamente un gruppo di persone si affrettò verso l’interno: in testa c’era Bergmann, barbuto e imponente, seguito da alcuni medici e assistenti. Mi gettai davanti a lui e dissi: “Sono venuto da migliaia di chilometri. Posso entrare?” Lui si fermò e mi fissò attraverso gli occhiali. “Forse vorresti prendere il mio posto, ” ringhiò, perdendo la calma in quella strana frenesia tipica della natura tedesca, “È l’unico posto disponibile. Sì, prendi pure il mio posto. Le mie lezioni sono già piene di inglesi, ” Pronunciò con rabbia la parola “inglesi”; in seguito appresi che una recente disputa con Morel MacKenzie riguardo alla malattia dell’imperatore Federico lo aveva molto infastidito. Fortunatamente mantenni la calma e il mio comportamento educato, che è sempre il miglior scudo quando si incontra brutale scortesia, “Assolutamente no,” dissi. “Non vorrei intrufolarmi, se davvero non c’è posto, ” Lui mi fissò di nuovo, poi proseguì con il suo gruppo, tutti sogghignanti per l’umiliazione subita da quel presuntuoso inglese. Uno di loro, tuttavia, si trattenne: un gentile americano. “Quel comportamento è stato davvero scortese,” disse. “Ascolta. Se ci incontriamo alle quattro di questo pomeriggio, ti mostrerò tutte le mie note della conferenza; conosco anche i casi che Bergmann intende presentare domani, quindi possiamo esaminarli insieme, ” Poi se ne andò.
Così accadde che alla fine raggiunsi la mia meta, ma in un modo indiretto. Studiai le lezioni e i casi analizzati, e ebbi l’audacia di dissentire da tutti, giungendo alla conclusione che tutto ciò fosse soltanto sperimentale e prematuro. Un’ondata di follia aveva invaso il mondo: da tutte le parti, soprattutto dall’Inghilterra, persone malate si affrettavano a Berlino in cerca di una cura; alcune di loro erano già in stadi così avanzati della malattia che morivano durante il viaggio in treno. Ero così convinto delle mie idee che scrissi una lettera di avvertimento al “Daily Telegraph”; credo proprio che quella fosse la prima lettera pubblicata con un tono di dubbio e cautela. Non c’è bisogno di dire che gli eventi dimostrarono la veridicità delle mie previsioni.  
Due giorni dopo tornai a Southsea, ma ero un uomo cambiato. Avevo scoperto le potenzialità nascoste in me stesso; in particolare, fui influenzato da una lunga conversazione con Malcolm Morris, che mi assicurò che stavo sprecando la mia vita nelle province e che avevo uno spazio troppo ristretto per le mie attività. Insistette affinché abbandonassi la pratica medica generale e andassi a Londra. Risposi che non ero ancora sicuro del mio successo letterario e che non potevo facilmente rinunciare alla carriera medica, che aveva richiesto tanti sacrifici da parte di mia madre e molti anni di studio da parte mia. Mi chiese se esistesse qualche branca specifica della medicina su cui potessi concentrarmi per evitare la pratica generale; dissi che negli ultimi anni mi ero interessato alla oftalmologia e avevo provato a correggere errori di rifrazione e prescrivere occhiali presso l’Ospedale Oftalmologico di Portsmouth, sotto la guida di Mr. Vernon Ford. “Beh,” disse Morris, “perché non specializzarti nell’oftalmologia? Vai a Vienna, dedica sei mesi allo studio, torna e inizia a lavorare a Londra. Così avrai una vita tranquilla e avrai molto tempo libero per dedicarti alla letteratura.” Tornai a casa con questa idea in mente; poiché mia moglie era d’accordo e Mary, la mia figlia, ormai abbastanza grande da poter stare con sua nonna, non sembrava esserci alcun ostacolo. Non ci furono difficoltà nel chiudere la pratica medica: era così piccola e di natura strettamente personale che semplicemente non poteva essere venduta a nessuno e dovette essere chiusa.
La Portsmouth Literary and Scientific Society mi organizzò un banchetto di addio. Ho molti ricordi piacevoli, e anche alcuni divertenti, legati a questa società di cui fui segretario per diversi anni. Durante i lunghi inverni, tenevamo vive la “fiamma sacra” della conoscenza attraverso le nostre riunioni settimanali e i dibattiti. Fu lì che imparai ad affrontare un pubblico, cosa che si rivelò di fondamentale importanza per il lavoro della mia vita. Naturalmente, inizialmente ero molto nervoso, timido e insicuro in queste situazioni; mi dissero che il segnale che indicava il mio imminente intervento nei dibattiti era il fatto che l’intera panca su cui sedevamo tremava a causa della mia emozione. Ma una volta salito sul palco, imparai a parlare con sicurezza, a nascondere le mie paure e a scegliere attentamente le parole da usare. Presentai tre relazioni: una sugli oceani artici, una su Carlyle e una su Gibbon. La prima mi valse una reputazione del tutto meritata di appassionato di sport, poiché presi in prestito dal taxidermista locale tutte le piante e gli animali che potessero trovarsi nell’Artico e li disposi sul tavolo dove tenevo i miei interventi. Il pubblico, deducendo che li avevo tutti cacciati personalmente, iniziò a guardarmi con grande rispetto. Ma la mattina seguente, quegli animali tornarono dal taxidermista! Durante questi dibattiti incontrammo anche persone strane e avvenimenti bizzarri. Ricordo in particolare una discussione molto approfondita sui fossili e sull’età delle formazioni geologiche, che terminò quando un generale maggiore di fede evangelica si alzò e dichiarò, con voce cupa, che tutta quella speculazione era vana e incomprensibile, poiché sapevamo, con certezza assoluta, che il mondo era stato creato esattamente cinquantamilaottocento novanta anni prima. Con questo, la discussione terminò e tutti noi tornammo a casa a dormire.
Il mio lavoro politico mi ha anche costretto ad imparare a parlare in pubblico. Ero considerato un Liberale-Unionista, cioè una persona la cui posizione generale era liberale, ma che non riusciva ad approvare la politica irlandese di Gladstone. Forse avevamo torto. Comunque, quella era la mia opinione all’epoca. Ebbi un’esperienza terribile nel parlare in pubblico su larga scala: durante un enorme raduno all’Anfiteatro, il candidato Sir William Crossman si ritardò, e per evitare un fiasco fui costretto ad affrontare un pubblico di 3.000 persone all’improvviso. Non sapevo quasi cosa stessi dicendo. Ma la parte irlandese di me intervenne in mio aiuto, fornendomi una serie di parole e metafore più o meno incoerenti che suscitarono grande entusiasmo nell’auditorio. Anche se, in seguito, quelle parole mi sembrarono più simili a un discorso comico che a un serio tentativo politico. Ma era esattamente ciò che volevano l’uditorio. E la maggior parte di loro si alzò in piedi prima ancora che finissi. Rimasi sorpreso quando lessi il testo il giorno dopo. Soprattutto l’ultima frase: “Inghilterra e Irlanda sono unite dal ‘anello nuziale di zaffiro del mare’; ciò che Dio ha unito, nessuno abbia il diritto di separare”. Non era una logica molto solida. Ma se si trattasse di eloquenza o di retorica, nemmeno ora riesco a stabilirlo con certezza.  
Quando il signor Balfour venne a tenere un discorso in un grande raduno, io ricoprivo la carica di segretario. Così, quando l’auditorium fu pieno, aspettai fuori per accoglierlo. Poco dopo arrivò la sua carrozza; scese, alto, magro e aristocratico. C’erano due noti sostenitori dell’opposizione ad attenderlo. Li avvertii di non creare problemi. Ma non appena Balfour apparve, uno di loro aprì la bocca per lanciare un grido di disprezzo. Ma non riuscì a farlo. Gli coprii rapidamente la bocca con una mano, tenendolo per il collo con l’altra. Il suo compagno mi colpì alla testa con un bastone, ma fu subito messo a terra da uno dei miei compagni. Intanto Balfour entrò sano e salvo nell’auditorium. E noi due segretari lo seguimmo, piuttosto disordinati dopo quell’avventura. In seguito incontrai più volte Lord Balfour. Ma non gli raccontai mai come avessi rischiato di perdere il cappello per difenderlo.
Con la Società Letteraria e i politici che frequentavo, lasciai un vuoto a Portsmouth. Così come mia moglie, molto amata per il suo carattere gentile e generoso. Fu difficile per noi lasciare così tanti buoni amici. Tuttavia, verso la fine del 1890, decidemmo di chiudere definitivamente Bush Villa. Trascorsi otto anni a Portsmouth, giorni di difficoltà, ma anche giorni di crescente successo. Ora, con un senso meraviglioso di libertà e avventura, iniziavamo una nuova fase della nostra vita.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_11_the_great_break" data-title="MEMORIES AND ADVENTURES — Chapter 10: THE GREAT BREAK" data-chapter="THE GREAT BREAK" data-kind="chapter" data-tags="setting/london,character/sherlock_holmes"></span>


CHAPTER X. THE GREAT BREAK
Vienna — A Specialist in Wimpole Street — The Great Decision — Norwood—” The Refugees “ — Reported Death of Holmes — Psychic Research Society — Literary Circles in [[settings/london|London]] — Henry Irving — A Great Blow—”Brigadier Gerard” — Davos — American Lecture Tour — Answer to Prayer.
WE set forth upon a bitter winter day at the close of 1890 with every chance of being snowed up on our long trek. We got through all right, however, and found ourselves in Vienna, arriving on a deadly cold night, with deep snow under foot and a cutting blizzard in the air. As we looked from the station the electric lights threw out the shining silver drift of snow-flakes against the absolute darkness of the sky. It was a gloomy, ominous reception, but half an hour afterwards when we were in the warm cosy crowded tobacco-laden restaurant attached to our hotel we took a more cheerful view of our surroundings.
We found a modest pension which was within our means, and we put in a very pleasant four months, during which I attended eye lectures at the Krankenhaus, but could certainly have learned far more in [[settings/london|London]], for even if one has a fair knowledge of conversational German it is very different from following accurately a rapid lecture filled with technical terms. No doubt “has studied in Vienna” sounds well in a specialist’s record, but it is usually taken for granted that he has exhausted his own country before going abroad, which was by no means the case with me. Therefore, so far as eye work goes, my winter was wasted, nor can I trace any particular spiritual or intellectual advance. On the other hand I saw a little of gay Viennese society. I received kind and welcome hospitality from Brinsley Richards, “The Times “correspondent, and his wife, and I had some excellent skating. I also wrote one short book, “The Doings of Raffles Haw,” not a very notable achievement, by which I was able to pay my current expenses without encroaching on the very few hundred pounds which were absolutely all that I had in the world. This money was invested on the advice of a friend, and as it was almost all lost — like so much more that I have earned — it is just as well that I was never driven back upon it.
With the spring my work at Vienna had finished, if it can be said to have ever begun, and we returned via Paris, putting in a few days there with Landolt, who was the most famous French oculist of his time. It was great to find ourselves back in [[settings/london|London]] once more with the feeling that we were now on the real field of battle, where we must conquer or perish, for our boats were burned behind us. It is easy now to look back and think that the issue was clear, but it was by no means so at the time, for I had earned little, though my reputation was growing. It was only my own inward conviction of the permanent merits of “The White Company,” still appearing month by month in “Cornhill,” which sustained my confidence. I had come through so much in the early days at Southsea that nothing could alarm me personally, but I had a wife and child now, and the stern simplicity of life which was possible and even pleasant in early days was now no longer to be thought of.
We took rooms in Montague Place, and I went forth to search for some place where I could put up my plate as an oculist. I was aware that many of the big men do not find time to work out refractions, which in some cases of astigmatism take a long time to adjust when done by retinoscopy. I was capable in this work and liked it, so I hoped that some of it might drift my way. But to get it, it was clearly necessary that I should live among the big men so that the patient could be easily referred to me. I searched the doctors’ quarters and at last found suitable accommodation at 2 Devonshire Place, which is at the top of Wimpole Street and close to the classical Harley Street. There for £120 a year I got the use of a front room with part use of a waiting-room. I was soon to find that they were both waiting-rooms, and now I know that it was better so.
Every morning I walked from the lodgings at Montague Place, reached my consulting-room at ten and sat there until three or four, with never a ring to disturb my serenity. Could better conditions for reflection and work be found? It was ideal, and so long as I was thoroughly unsuccessful in my professional venture there was every chance of improvement in my literary prospects Therefore when I returned to the lodgings at tea-time I bore my little sheaves with me, the first-fruits of a considerable harvest.
A number of monthly magazines were coming out at that time, notable among which was “The Strand,” then as now under the editorship of Greenhough Smith. Considering these various journals with their disconnected stories it had struck me that a single character running through a series, if it only engaged the attention of the reader, would bind that reader to that particular magazine. On the other hand, it had long seemed to me that the ordinary serial might be an impediment rather than a help to a magazine, since, sooner or later, one missed one number and afterwards it had lost all interest. Clearly the ideal compromise was a character which carried through, and yet instalments which were each complete in themselves, so that the purchaser was always sure that he could relish the whole contents of the magazine. I believe that I was the first to realise this and “The Strand Magazine “the first to put it into practice.
Looking round for my central character I felt that [[characters/sherlock-holmes|Sherlock Holmes]], whom I had already handled in two little books, would easily lend himself to a succession of short stories. These I began in the long hours of waiting in my consulting-room. Greenhough Smith liked them from the first, and encouraged me to go ahead with them. My literary affairs had been taken up by that king of agents, A. P. Watt, who relieved me of all the hateful bargaining, and handled things so well that any immediate anxiety for money soon disappeared. It was as well, for not one single patient had ever crossed the threshold of my room.
I was now once more at a crossroads of my life, and Providence, which I recognise at every step, made me realise it in a very energetic and unpleasant way. I was starting off for my usual trudge one morning from our lodgings when icy shivers passed over me, and I only got back in time to avoid a total collapse. It was a virulent attack of influenza, at a time when influenza was in its deadly prime. Only three years before my dear sister Annette, after spending her whole life on the family needs, had died of it at Lisbon at the very moment when my success would have enabled me to recall her from her long servitude. Now it was my turn, and I very nearly followed her. I can remember no pain or extreme discomfort, and no psychic experiences, but for a week I was in great danger, and then found myself as weak as a child and as emotional, but with a mind as clear as crystal. It was then, as I surveyed my own life, that I saw how foolish I was to waste my literary earnings in keeping up an oculist’s room in Wimpole Street, and I determined with a wild rush of joy to cut the painter and to trust for ever to my power of writing. I remember in my delight taking the handkerchief which lay upon the coverlet in my enfeebled hand, and tossing it up to the ceiling in my exultation.
I should at last be my own master. No longer would I have to conform to professional dress or try to please any one else. I would be free to live how I liked and where I liked. It was one of the great moments of exultation of my life. The date was in August, 1891.
Presently I was about, hobbling on a stick and reflecting that if I lived to be eighty I knew already exactly how it would feel. I haunted house-agents, got lists of suburban villas, and spent some weeks, as my strength returned, in searching for a new home. Finally I found a suitable house, modest but comfortable, isolated and yet one of a row. It was 12 Tennison Road, South Norwood. There we settled down, and there I made my first effort to live entirely by my pen. It soon became evident that I had been playing the game well within my powers and that I should have no difficulty in providing a sufficient income. It seemed as if I had settled into a life which might be continuous, and I little foresaw that an unexpected blow was about to fall upon us, and that we were not at the end, but really at the beginning, of our wanderings.
I could not know this, however, and I settled down with a stout heart to do some literary work worthy of the name. The difficulty of the Holmes work was that every story really needed as clear-cut and original a plot as a longish book would do. One cannot without effort spin plots at such a rate. They are apt to become thin or to break. I was determined, now that I had no longer the excuse of absolute pecuniary pressure, never again to write anything which was not as good as I could possibly make it, and therefore I would not write a Holmes story without a worthy plot and without a problem which interested my own mind, for that is the first requisite before you can interest any one else. If I have been able to sustain this character for a long time and if the public find, as they will find, that the last story is as good as the first, it is entirely due to the fact that I never, or hardly ever, forced a story. Some have thought there was a falling off in the stories, and the criticism was neatly expressed by a Cornish boatman who said to me, “I think, sir, when Holmes fell over that cliff, he may not have killed himself, but all the same he was never quite the same man afterwards.” I think, however, that if the reader began the series backwards, so that he brought a fresh mind to the last stories, he would agree with me that, though the general average may not be conspicuously high, still the last one is as good as the first.
I was weary, however, of inventing plots and I set myself now to do some work which would certainly be less remunerative but would be more ambitious from a literary point of view. I had long been attracted by the epoch of Louis XIV and by those Huguenots who were the French equivalents of our Puritans. I had a good knowledge of the memoirs of that date, and many notes already prepared, so that it did not take me long to write “The Refugees.” It has stood the acid test of time very well, so I may say that it was a success. Soon after its appearance it was translated into French, and my dear old mother, herself a great French scholar, had the joy when she visited Fontainebleau to hear the official guide tell the drove of tourists that if they really wanted to know about the Court of the great monarch, they would find the clearest and most accurate account in an Englishman’s book, “The Refugees.” I expect the guide would have been considerably astonished had he then and there been kissed by an elderly English lady, but it was an experience which he must have narrowly missed. I used in this book, also, a great deal which was drawn from Parkman, that great but neglected historian, who was in my opinion the greatest serious writer that America has produced.
There was an amusing episode connected with “The Refugees,” when it was read aloud in some strict Irish convent, the innocent Reverend Mother having mistaken my name and imagined that I was a canon, and therefore of course a holy man. I am told that the reading was a tremendous success and that the good sisters rejoiced that the mistake was not found out until the story was completed. My first name has several times led to mistakes, as when, at a big dinner at Chicago, I was asked to say Grace, as being the only ecclesiastic present. I remember that at the same dinner one of the speakers remarked that it was a most sinister fact that though I was a doctor no living patient of mine had ever yet been seen.
During this Norwood interval, I was certainly working hard, for besides “The Refugees” I wrote “The Great Shadow,” a booklet which I should put near the front of my work for merit, and two other little books on a very inferior plane—” The Parasite “and “Beyond the City.” The latter was of a domestic type unusual for me. It was pirated in New York just before the New Copyright Act came into force, and the rascal publisher thinking that a portrait — any sort of portrait — of the author would look well upon the cover, and being quite ignorant of my identity, put a very pretty and over-dressed young woman as my presentment. I still preserve a copy of this most flattering representation. All these books had some decent success, though none of it was remarkable. It was still the [[characters/sherlock-holmes|Sherlock Holmes]] stories for which the public clamoured, and these from time to time I endeavoured to supply. At last, after I had done two series of them I saw that I was in danger of having my hand forced, and of being entirely identified with what I regarded as a lower stratum of literary achievement. Therefore as a sign of my resolution I determined to end the life of my hero. The idea was in my mind when I went with my wife for a short holiday in Switzerland, in the course of which we saw there the wonderful falls of Reichenbach, a terrible place, and one that I thought would make a worthy tomb for poor Sherlock, even if I buried my banking account along with him. So there I laid him, fully determined that he should stay there — as indeed for some years he did. I was amazed at the concern expressed by the public. They say that a man is never properly appreciated until he is dead, and the general protest against my summary execution of Holmes taught me how many and how numerous were his friends. “You Brute “was the beginning of the letter of remonstrance which one lady sent me, and I expect she spoke for others besides herself. I heard of many who wept. I fear I was utterly callous myself, and only glad to have a chance of opening out into new fields of imagination, for the temptation of high prices made it difficult to get one’s thoughts away from Holmes.
That [[characters/sherlock-holmes|Sherlock Holmes]] was anything but mythical to many is shown by the fact that I have had many letters addressed to him with requests that I forward them. Watson has also had a number of letters in which he has been asked for the address or for the autograph of his more brilliant confrère. A press-cutting agency wrote to Watson asking whether Holmes would not wish to subscribe. When Holmes retired several elderly ladies were ready to keep house for him and one sought to ingratiate herself by assuring me that she knew all about bee-keeping and could “segregate the queen.” I had considerable offers also for Holmes if he would examine and solve various family mysteries. Once the offer — from Poland — was that I should myself go, and my reward was practically left to my own judgment. I had judgment enough, however, to avoid it altogether.
I have often been asked whether I had myself the qualities which I depicted, or whether I was merely the Watson that I look. Of course I am well aware that it is one thing to grapple with a practical problem and quite another thing when you are allowed to solve it under your own conditions. I have no delusions about that. At the same time a man cannot spin a character out of his own inner consciousness and make it really life-like unless he has some possibilities of that character within him — which is a dangerous admission for one who has drawn so many villains as I. In my poem “The Inner Room,” describing our multiplex personality, I say:
“There are others who are sitting, Grim as doom, In the dim ill-boding shadow Of my room. Darkling figures, stern or quaint, Now a savage, now a saint, Showing fitfully and faint In the gloom.”
Among those figures there may perhaps be an astute detective also, but I find that in real life in order to find him I have to inhibit all the others and get into a mood when there is no one in the room but he. Then I get results and have several times solved problems by Holmes’ methods after the police have been baffled. Yet I must admit that in ordinary life I am by no means observant and that I have to throw myself into an artificial frame of mind before I can weigh evidence and anticipate the sequence of events.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

**CAPITOLO X. LA GRANDE DECISIONE**  
Vienna – Un specialista in Wimpole Street – La grande decisione – Norwood – “I rifugiati” – Si annuncia la morte di Holmes – Società di ricerca psichica – Circoli letterari a [[settings/london|Londra]] – Henry Irving – Un duro colpo – “Il brigadiere Gerard” – Davos – Tour di conferenze negli Stati Uniti – Risposta a una preghiera. Partimmo in un freddo giorno d’inverno alla fine del 1890, con ogni probabilità di rimanere bloccati dalla neve durante il lungo viaggio. Tuttavia riuscimmo ad arrivare sani e salvi a Vienna, in una notte terribilmente fredda, con la neve alta fino alle caviglie e un forte vento gelido. Guardando fuori dalla stazione, le luci elettriche illuminavano i fiocchi di neve che si stagliavano contro l’oscurità del cielo. Fu un’accoglienza cupa e infausta. Ma mezz’ora dopo, trovandoci nel caldo e accogliente ristorante del nostro hotel, iniziammo a vedere il mondo con occhi più ottimisti. Trovammo una pensione modesta che ci andava bene e trascorremmo quattro mesi molto piacevoli. Durante quel periodo assistetti a lezioni di oftalmologia all’ospedale, ma avrei potuto imparare molto di più a [[settings/london|Londra]]. Anche se si conosce abbastanza il tedesco parlato, è molto diverso dal seguire attentamente una lezione tecnica piena di termini specialistici. Senza dubbio, “aver studiato a Vienna” suona bene nel curriculum di un specialista. Ma di solito si presuppone che abbia già esaurito tutte le opportunità nel proprio paese prima di andare all’estero. Il che non era affatto il mio caso. Quindi, per quanto riguarda la mia formazione in ambito oftalmologico, quell’inverno è stato sprecato. E non posso registrare alcun progresso spirituale o intellettuale particolare. D’altra parte, ebbi l’opportunità di conoscere un po’ della vivace società viennese: ricevetti ospitalità gentile da Brinsley Richards, corrispondente del “The Times”, e sua moglie; inoltre feci del ottimo pattinaggio. Scrissi anche un breve libro, “Le avventure di Raffles Haw”. Un risultato non molto significativo, ma sufficiente a coprire le mie spese senza indebitarmi ulteriormente. Quei poche centinaia di sterline che avevo erano tutto ciò che possedevo al mondo. E furono investite su consiglio di un amico. Peccato che siano andate quasi tutte perse. Proprio come molte altre cose che ho guadagnato. Meglio così, forse.
Con l’arrivo della primavera, il mio lavoro a Vienna era terminato, se si può davvero dire che fosse mai iniziato. Tornammo quindi via Parigi, trascorrendo alcuni giorni lì con Landolt, il più famoso oculista francese dell’epoca. Fu meraviglioso ritrovarsi di nuovo a [[settings/london|Londra]], con la sensazione di essere finalmente nel vero campo di battaglia: dove avremmo dovuto vincere o perdere, poiché le nostre “navi” erano state distrutte. Ora è facile ripensare a quei tempi e credere che la situazione fosse chiara; ma all’epoca non lo era affatto. Avevo guadagnato poco, anche se la mia reputazione stava crescendo. Fu solo la mia ferma convinzione nel valore di “La Compagnia Bianca”, che continuava ad apparire ogni mese su “Cornhill”, a mantenermi fiducioso. Avevo già superato tante difficoltà nei primi giorni a Southsea, quindi nulla poteva più spaventarmi personalmente; ma ora avevo una moglie e un figlio, e quella semplicità di vita che un tempo era possibile, non poteva più essere considerata una soluzione adatta. Prendemmo degli appartamenti in Montague Place, e io iniziai a cercare un posto dove poter esercitare la mia professione di oculista. Sapevo che molti medici importanti non trovavano il tempo necessario per effettuare le misurazioni oculari, soprattutto in casi di astigmatismo, dove l’uso della retinoscopia richiedeva molto tempo. Io ero abile in questo lavoro e mi piaceva, quindi speravo che qualche opportunità potesse presentarsi. Ma per ottenerla, era necessario vivere tra quei medici importanti, in modo che i pazienti potessero essere facilmente indirizzati a me. Dopo molte ricerche, trovai un posto adatto in 2 Devonshire Place: situato all’inizio di Wimpole Street, vicino alla famosa Harley Street. Per 120 sterline all’anno, potevo utilizzare un soggiorno e parte di una sala d’attesa. Anche se presto scoprii che entrambe le stanze erano effettivamente sale d’attesa, il che, in realtà, era anche meglio. Ogni mattina camminavo da Montague Place fino al mio studio, dove restavo seduto dalle dieci alle tre o quattro del pomeriggio, senza che nessun suono interrompesse la mia tranquillità. Esistevano condizioni migliori per riflettere e lavorare? Era perfetto. E finché non avessi avuto successo nella mia carriera professionale, c’erano tutte le possibilità di migliorare nelle mie attività letterarie. Quindi, quando tornavo agli appartamenti a ora di tè, portavo con me i primi frutti del mio lavoro, i risultati delle mie fatiche.
In quel periodo uscivano numerose riviste mensili; tra queste spiccava “The Strand”, allora come oggi sotto la direzione di Greenhough Smith. Considerando tutte queste pubblicazioni e i loro racconti sparsi, mi era venuta l’idea che un personaggio fisso che attraversasse più storie, se solo riuscisse a catturare l’attenzione del lettore, potesse legarlo saldamente a quella rivista. D’altra parte, mi sembrava da tempo che una serie regolare potesse rappresentare un ostacolo piuttosto che un aiuto per una rivista: infatti, prima o poi si finiva per perdere un numero e, di conseguenza, ogni interesse per essa svaniva. L’equilibrio ideale, quindi, consisteva in un personaggio che continuasse ad apparire nelle varie storie, ma in episodi ciascuno autonomo, in modo che il lettore fosse sempre sicuro di poter godere appieno del contenuto della rivista. Credo di essere stato il primo a rendersene conto, e “The Strand Magazine” il primo ad attuarlo concretamente. Cercando il personaggio principale per la mia serie, pensai subito a [[characters/sherlock-holmes|Sherlock Holmes]], che avevo già utilizzato in due racconti brevi; decisi quindi di iniziare a scrivere queste storie durante le lunghe ore trascorse nel mio studio. Greenhough Smith le apprezzò fin dall’inizio e mi incoraggiò ad andare avanti. I miei affari letterari erano ormai gestiti da A. P. Watt, quel geniale agente che mi risparmiò tutti gli spiacevoli accordi finanziari e si occupò di tutto in modo impeccabile; così, qualsiasi preoccupazione legata ai soldi svanì rapidamente. Anzi, nessun paziente entrò mai nel mio studio! Ora mi trovavo di nuovo di fronte a una svolta importante nella mia vita, e la Provvidenza me lo fece capire in modo molto drammatico. Una mattina, mentre stavo per partire per il solito tragitto, fui assalito da brividi intensi; riuscii appena in tempo a evitare di cadere completamente privo di forze. Si trattava di un attacco violento di influenza, in un periodo in cui questa malattia era particolarmente mortale. Solo tre anni prima mia cara sorella Annette, dopo aver dedicato tutta la sua vita alle esigenze della famiglia, era morta a Lisbona proprio nel momento in cui il mio successo avrebbe potuto permettermi di riportarla a casa. Ora toccava a me. Per una settimana fui in grave pericolo, ma poi mi ritrovai debole come un bambino, molto emotivo, ma con la mente lucida come il cristallo. Fu allora che, riflettendo sulla mia vita, capii quanto fosse stupido sprecare i miei guadagni letterari mantenendo uno studio di oculista in Wimpole Street. E decisi, con grande gioia, di affidarmi completamente alla mia capacità di scrivere. Ricordo ancora di aver preso il fazzoletto che era sul copriletto con la mia mano debole e di averlo gettato verso il soffitto, esultante.
Finalmente avrei potuto essere il padrone di me stesso. Non avrei più dovuto conformarmi alle regole dell’abbigliamento professionale né cercare di compiacere gli altri. Sarei stato libero di vivere come volevo e dove volevo. Fu uno dei momenti più gioiosi della mia vita. La data? Agosto 1891.  
In quel momento, zoppicando su un bastone, riflettevo che, se fossi vissuto fino agli ottant’anni, avrei già saputo esattamente com’era quella sensazione. Iniziai a cercare case nei dintorni di Londra, ottenni delle liste di ville suburbane e, man mano che riprendevo le forze, passai alcune settimane a cercare una nuova dimora. Alla fine ne trovai una adatta: modesta ma confortevole, isolata, ma parte di una fila di case. Era situata in 12 Tennison Road, South Norwood. Lì ci stabilimmo e lì feci il mio primo tentativo di vivere interamente grazie alla mia scrittura. Presto mi resi conto che stavo riuscendo nel mio intento e che non avrei avuto difficoltà a guadagnare abbastanza. Sembrava che fossi entrato in una vita stabile. Ma non immaginavo affatto che un colpo inaspettato ci attendesse. E che, in realtà, eravamo appena all’inizio dei nostri “vagabondaggi”.  
Non potevo saperlo, però. E con determinazione mi misi al lavoro, deciso a creare opere letterarie degne di questo nome. Il problema principale legato alla serie di storie su Holmes era che ogni racconto richiedeva una trama chiara e originale, proprio come avrebbe richiesto un libro più lungo. Non è facile inventare tante trame in così poco tempo. Spesso queste diventano banali o si rompono. Ora che non avevo più scuse legate alle pressioni finanziarie, ero deciso a non scrivere mai nulla di meno di ciò che potevo offrire al meglio. Quindi non avrei scritto una storia su Holmes senza una trama valida e senza un problema che interessasse davvero la mia mente. Questo è infatti il primo requisito per riuscire a interessare anche gli altri lettori. Se sono riuscito a mantenere questo standard per così tanto tempo, e se il pubblico ha trovato le ultime storie altrettanto buone come le prime, è tutto grazie al fatto che non ho mai, o quasi mai, forzato la realizzazione delle mie idee. Alcuni hanno pensato che le storie diventassero meno interessanti con il passare del tempo. Un barcaiolo del Galles mi disse: “Penso che, quando Holmes è caduto da quel dirupo, forse non si sia suicidato. Ma comunque, dopo quell’incidente, non è più stato lo stesso, ” Io credo invece che, se i lettori iniziassero a leggere la serie dall’ultimo racconto verso il primo, noterebbero che, anche se l’insieme non è eccezionalmente “alto”, l’ultimo episodio è comunque altrettanto buono come il primo.
Ero però stanco di inventare storie e decisi quindi di dedicarmi a un lavoro che, sebbene meno remunerativo, fosse più ambizioso dal punto di vista letterario. Da tempo ero affascinato dall’epoca di Luigi XIV e da quegli Ugonotti che rappresentavano in Francia l’equivalente dei nostri Puritani. Conoscevo bene i ricordi di quel periodo e avevo già preparato molte note, quindi non mi ci volle molto per scrivere “I Rifugiati”. Questo libro ha resistito molto bene al passare del tempo, quindi posso dire che sia stato un successo. Poco dopo la sua pubblicazione fu tradotto in francese, e mia cara madre, che era una grande studiosa di francese, ebbe la gioia di sentire il guida turistico dire ai gruppi di visitatori che, se volevano davvero conoscere qualcosa della corte di quel grande monarca, avrebbero trovato la descrizione più chiara e accurata in un libro scritto da un inglese: “I Rifugiati”. Immagino che il guida sarebbe rimasto molto sorpreso se in quel momento fosse stato baciato da una signora anziana inglese. Ma è stata un’esperienza che, probabilmente, gli è sfuggita per un soffio. In questo libro ho anche utilizzato molti materiali tratti dalle opere di Parkman, quel grande ma trascurato storico che, a mio parere, è stato il più importante scrittore serio prodotto dall’America.  
Ci fu anche un episodio divertente legato a “I Rifugiati”: quando venne letto ad alta voce in un rigido convento irlandese, la pura e innocente madre badessa confondette il mio nome e pensò che fossi un canonico, quindi ovviamente una persona santa. Mi è stato detto che la lettura ebbe un enorme successo e che le buone suore furono felici che l’errore venisse scoperto solo alla fine del libro. Il mio nome ha già causato più volte simili confusioni: ad esempio, durante una grande cena a Chicago, mi chiesero di recitare la preghiera di ringraziamento, poiché ero l’unico ecclesiastico presente. Ricordo che durante quella stessa cena uno degli intervenuti osservò che era davvero strano il fatto che, nonostante fossi un medico, nessuno dei miei pazienti fosse mai morto.
Durante questo periodo, lavoravo sodo: oltre a “I Rifugiati”, scrissi anche “L’Ombra Immensa”, un libretto che meriterebbe di essere messo tra le mie opere più importanti, e altre due piccole opere di livello molto inferiore: “Il Parassita” e “Oltre la Città”. Quest’ultima aveva un tema domestico, insolito per me. Fu piratata a New York poco prima che entrasse in vigore il nuovo diritto d’autore; quel furfante di editore, pensando che una fotografia dell’autore – qualsiasi tipo di foto – sarebbe stata adatta per la copertina, e ignorando completamente chi fossi io, utilizzò l’immagine di una giovane donna molto attraente ma eccessivamente vestita come mia rappresentazione. Ancora oggi conservo quella fotografia. Tutti questi libri ebbero un certo successo, anche se nessuno di essi fu davvero eccezionale. Il pubblico continuava ad attendere con impazienza le storie di [[characters/sherlock-holmes|Sherlock Holmes]], e io cercavo di soddisfare questa richiesta ogni volta che ne avevo l’opportunità. Alla fine, dopo averne scritto due serie, mi resi conto che rischiavo di essere identificato esclusivamente con quel genere letterario, che ritenevo di scarso valore. Così, come segno della mia determinazione, decisi di porre fine alla “vita” del mio eroe. Questa idea mi venne in mente mentre trascorrevo una breve vacanza in Svizzera, dove vedemmo le meravigliose cascate di Reichenbach. Un luogo terribile. Pensai che sarebbe stato un ottimo sepolcro per povero Sherlock. Così lo “seppellii” lì, deciso che vi rimanesse per sempre. E infatti così fu per molti anni. Fui sorpreso dall’attenzione che il pubblico dimostrò per questa decisione. Si dice che un uomo venga veramente apprezzato solo dopo la sua morte. La generale protesta contro la mia “giustizia sommaria” nei confronti di Holmes mi fece capire quanti fossero i suoi amici, “Brutto animale, ”. Era l’inizio della lettera di rimprovero che una signora mi inviò. E credo che rappresentasse anche il pensiero di molti altri. Sentii parlare di molte persone che avevano pianto. Temo di essere stato davvero insensibile. Ero semplicemente felice di avere l’opportunità di esplorare nuovi campi dell’immaginazione. La tentazione dei grandi guadagni, infatti, rendeva difficile allontanare i miei pensieri da Sherlock Holmes.
Il fatto che [[characters/sherlock-holmes|Sherlock Holmes]] non fosse affatto una figura mitica per molte persone è dimostrato dal gran numero di lettere che ricevo indirizzate a lui, con richieste di farle avere a lui stesso. Anche Watson ha ricevuto diverse lettere in cui gli chiedevano l’indirizzo o l’autografo del suo più brillante collega. Un’agenzia di stampa ha scritto a Watson chiedendogli se Holmes non desiderasse iscriversi a qualche servizio. Quando Holmes si ritirò, diverse signore anziane erano disposte ad occuparsi delle sue necessità domestiche; una di loro cercò persino di farsi apprezzare assicurandomi di conoscere molto sull’apicoltura e di essere in grado di “separare la regina dalle altre api”. Ho ricevuto anche molte offerte per Holmes, nel caso volesse esaminare e risolvere vari misteri familiari. Una volta, un’offerta proveniente dalla Polonia prevedeva addirittura che fossi io ad andarci personalmente, con la ricompensa lasciata interamente a mia discrezione. Tuttavia, ho avuto abbastanza buon senso da rifiutare del tutto. Mi è stato spesso chiesto se possedessi davvero le qualità che descrivo nei miei racconti, o se fossi semplicemente il “Watson” che appaio. Ovviamente so bene che affrontare un problema pratico è una cosa, mentre risolverlo nelle proprie condizioni è tutta un’altra. Non ho alcuna illusione al riguardo. Allo stesso tempo, un uomo non può creare un personaggio partendo esclusivamente dalla propria coscienza interiore e renderlo verosimile, a meno che non possieda realmente in sé quelle caratteristiche. Il che rappresenta una confessione pericolosa, soprattutto per uno che ha creato così tanti personaggi malvagi come Holmes. Nel mio poema “La stanza interna”, che descrive la nostra personalità multipla, dico: “Ci sono altri che sedono lì, cupi e minacciosi, nell’oscura ombra della mia stanza. Figure oscure, severe o strane: ora selvagge, ora sante. Appaiono e scompaiono nella penombra.” Tra quelle figure, forse c’è anche un detective astuto. Ma nella vita reale, per trovarlo devo reprimere tutte le altre emozioni e immergermi in uno stato mentale in cui nella stanza non ci sia nessuno se non lui. Solo allora ottengo risultati: ho risolto diversi casi utilizzando i metodi di Holmes, dopo che la polizia si era rivelata incapace di farlo. Tuttavia devo ammettere che nella vita quotidiana non sono affatto osservatore attento. Devo immergermi in uno stato mentale artificiale per poter valutare le prove e prevedere l’evolversi degli eventi.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_12_sidelights_on_sherlock_holmes" data-title="MEMORIES AND ADVENTURES — Chapter 11: SIDELIGHTS ON SHERLOCK HOLMES" data-chapter="SIDELIGHTS ON SHERLOCK HOLMES" data-kind="chapter" data-tags="setting/edinburgh,setting/london,character/sherlock_holmes"></span>


CHAPTER XI. SIDELIGHTS ON [[characters/sherlock-holmes|SHERLOCK HOLMES]]
“The Speckled Band” — Barrie’s Parody on Holmes — Holmes on the Films — Methods of Construction — Problems — Curious Letters — Some Personal Cases — Strange Happenings.
I MAY as well interrupt my narrative here in order to say what may interest my readers about my most notorious character.
The impression that Holmes was a real person of flesh and blood may have been intensified by his frequent appearance upon the stage. After the withdrawal of my dramatization of “Rodney Stone “from a theatre upon which I held a six months’ lease, I determined to play a bold and energetic game, for an empty theatre spells ruin. When I saw the course that things were taking I shut myself up and devoted my whole mind to making a sensational [[characters/sherlock-holmes|Sherlock Holmes]] drama. I wrote it in a week and called it “The Speckled Band “after the short story of that name. I do not think that I exaggerate if I say that within a fortnight of the one play shutting down I had a company working upon the rehearsals of a second one, which had been written in the interval. It was a considerable success. Lyn Harding, as the half epileptic and wholly formidable Doctor Grimesby Rylott, was most masterful, while Saintsbury as [[characters/sherlock-holmes|Sherlock Holmes]] was also very good. Before the end of the run I had cleared off all that I had lost upon the other play, and I had created a permanent property of some value. It became a stock piece and is even now touring the country. We had a fine rock boa to play the title-role, a snake which was the pride of my heart, so one can imagine my disgust when I saw that one critic ended his disparaging review by the words “The crisis of the play was produced by the appearance of a palpably artificial serpent.” I was inclined to offer him a goodly sum if he would undertake to go to bed with it. We had several snakes at different times, but they were none of them born actors and they were all inclined either to hang down from the hole in the wall like inanimate bell-pulls, or else to turn back through the hole and get even with the stage carpenter who pinched their tails in order to make them more lively. Finally we used artificial snakes, and every one, including the stage carpenter, agreed that it was more satisfactory.
This was the second Sherlock Holmes play. I should have spoken about the first, which was produced very much earlier, in fact at the time of the African war. It was written and most wonderfully acted by William Gillette, the famous American. Since he used my characters and to some extent my plots, he naturally gave me a share in the undertaking, which proved to be very successful. “May I marry Holmes?” was one cable which I received from him when in the throes of composition. “You may marry or murder or do what you like with him,” was my heartless reply. I was charmed both with the play, the acting and the pecuniary result. I think that every man with a drop of artistic blood in his veins would agree that the latter consideration, though very welcome when it does arrive, is still the last of which he thinks.
Sir James Barrie paid his respects to Sherlock Holmes in a rollicking parody. It was really a gay gesture of resignation over the failure which we had encountered with a comic opera for which he undertook to write the libretto. I collaborated with him on this, but in spite of our joint efforts, the piece fell flat. Whereupon Barrie sent me a parody on Holmes, written on the fly leaves of one of his books. It ran thus: —
The Adventure of the Two Collaborators In bringing to a close the adventures of my friend Sherlock Holmes I am perforce reminded that he never, save on the occasion which, as you will now hear, brought his singular career to an end, consented to act in any mystery which was concerned with persons who made a livelihood by their pen. “I am not particular about the people I mix among for business purposes,” he would say, “but at literary characters I draw the line.”
We were in our rooms in Baker Street one evening. I was (I remember) by the centre table writing out “The Adventure of the Man without a Cork Leg “(which had so puzzled the Royal Society and all the other scientific bodies of Europe), and Holmes was amusing himself with a little revolver practice. It was his custom of a summer evening to fire round my head, just shaving my face, until he had made a photograph of me on the opposite wall, and it is a slight proof of his skill that many of these portraits in pistol shots are considered admirable likenesses.
I happened to look out of the window, and perceiving two gentlemen advancing rapidly along Baker Street asked him who they were. He immediately lit his pipe, and, twisting himself on a chair into the figure 8, replied:
“They are two collaborators in comic opera, and their play has not been a triumph.”
I sprang from my chair to the ceiling in amazement, and he then explained:
“My dear Watson, they are obviously men who follow some low calling. That much even you should be able to read in their faces. Those little pieces of blue paper which they fling angrily from them are Durrant’s Press Notices. Of these they have obviously hundreds about their person (see how their pockets bulge). They would not dance on them if they were pleasant reading.”
I again sprang to the ceiling (which is much dented), and shouted: “Amazing! but they may be mere authors.”
“No,” said Holmes, “for mere authors only get one press notice a week. Only criminals, dramatists and actors get them by the hundred.”
“Then they may be actors.”
“No, actors would come in a carriage.”
“Can you tell me anything else about them?”
“A great deal. From the mud on the boots of the tall one I perceive that he comes from South Norwood. The other is as obviously a Scotch author.”
“How can you tell that?”
“He is carrying in his pocket a book called (I clearly see) ‘Auld Licht Something.’ Would any one but the author be likely to carry about a book with such a title?”
I had to confess that this was improbable.
It was now evident that the two men (if such they can be called) were seeking our lodgings. I have said (often) that my friend Holmes seldom gave way to emotion of any kind, but he now turned livid with passion. Presently this gave place to a strange look of triumph.
“Watson,” he said, “that big fellow has for years taken the credit for my most remarkable doings, but at last I have him — at last!”
Up I went to the ceiling, and when I returned the strangers were in the room.
“I perceive, gentlemen,” said Mr. Sherlock Holmes, “that you are at present afflicted by an extraordinary novelty.”
The handsomer of our visitors asked in amazement how he knew this, but the big one only scowled.
“You forget that you wear a ring on your fourth finger,” replied Mr. Holmes calmly.
I was about to jump to the ceiling when the big brute interposed.
“That Tommy-rot is all very well for the public, Holmes,” said he, “but you can drop it before me. And, Watson, if you go up to the ceiling again I shall make you stay there.”
Here I observed a curious phenomenon. My friend Sherlock Holmes shrank. He became small before my eyes. I looked longingly at the ceiling, but dared not.
“Let us cut the first four pages,” said the big man, “and proceed to business. I want to know why—”
“Allow me,” said Mr. Holmes, with some of his old courage. “You want to know why the public does not go to your opera.”
“Exactly,” said the other ironically, “as you perceive by my shirt stud.” He added more gravely, “And as you can only find out in one way I must insist on your witnessing an entire performance of the piece.”
It was an anxious moment for me. I shuddered, for I knew that if Holmes went I should have to go with him. But my friend had a heart of gold. “Never,” he cried fiercely, “I will do anything for you save that.”
“Your continued existence depends on it,” said the big man menacingly.
“I would rather melt into air,” replied Holmes, proudly taking another chair. “But I can tell you why the public don’t go to your piece without sitting the thing out myself.”
“Why?”
“Because,” replied Holmes calmly, “they prefer to stay away.”
A dead silence followed that extraordinary remark. For a moment the two intruders gazed with awe upon the man who had unravelled their mystery so wonderfully. Then drawing their knives —
Holmes grew less and less, until nothing was left save a ring of smoke which slowly circled to the ceiling.
The last words of great men are often noteworthy. These were the last words of Sherlock Holmes: “Fool, fool! I have kept you in luxury for years. By my help you have ridden extensively in cabs, where no author was ever seen before. Henceforth you will ride in buses!”
The brute sunk into a chair aghast.
The other author did not turn a hair.
To A. Conan Doyle, from his friend J. M. Barrie.
This parody, the best of all the numerous parodies, may be taken as an example not only of the author’s wit but of his debonair courage, for it was written immediately after our joint failure which at the moment was a bitter thought for both of us. There is indeed nothing more miserable than a theatrical failure, for you feel how many others who have backed you have been affected by it. It was, I am glad to say, my only experience of it, and I have no doubt that Barrie could say the same.
Before I leave the subject of the many impersonations of Holmes I may say that all of them, and all the drawings, are very unlike my own original idea of the man. I saw him as very tall—” over 6 feet, but so excessively lean that he seemed considerably taller,” said “A Study in Scarlet.” He had, as I imagined him, a thin razor-like face, with a great hawks-bill of a nose, and two small eyes, set close I together on either side of it. Such was my conception. It chanced, however, that poor Sidney Paget who, before his premature death, drew all the original pictures, had a younger brother whose name, I think, I was Walter, who served him as a model. The handsome Walter took the place of the more powerful but uglier Sherlock, and perhaps from the point of view of my lady readers it was as well. The stage has I followed the type set up by the pictures.
Films of course were unknown when the stories appeared, and when these rights were finally discussed and a small sum offered for them by a French Company it seemed treasure trove and I was very glad to accept. Afterwards I had to buy them back again at exactly ten times what I had received, so the deal was a disastrous one. But now they have been done; by the Stoll Company with Eille Norwood as Holmes,  and it was worth all the expense to get so fine a production. Norwood has since played the part on the; stage and won the approbation of the [[settings/london|London]] public. | He has that rare quality which can only be described as glamour, which compels you to watch an actor eagerly even when he is doing nothing. He has the brooding eye which excites expectation and he has also a quite unrivalled power of disguise. My only criticism of the films is that they introduce telephones, motor cars and other luxuries of which the Victorian Holmes never dreamed.
People have often asked me whether I knew the end of a Holmes story before I started it. Of course I do. One could not possibly steer a course if one did not know one’s destination. The first thing is to get your idea. Having got that key idea one’s next task is to conceal it and lay emphasis upon everything which can make for a different explanation. Holmes, however, can see all the fallacies of the alternatives, and arrives more or less dramatically at the true solution by steps which he can describe and justify. He shows his powers by what the South Americans now call “Sherlockholmitos,” which means clever little deductions, which often have nothing to do with the matter in hand, but impress the reader with a general sense of power. The same effect is gained by his offhand allusion to other cases. Heaven knows how many titles I have thrown about in a casual way, and how many readers have begged me to satisfy their curiosity as to “Rigoletto and his abominable wife,” “The Adventure of the Tired Captain,” or “The Curious Experience of the Patterson Family in the Island of Uffa.” Once or twice, as in “The Adventure of the Second Stain,” which in my judgment is one of the neatest of the stories, I did actually use the title years before I wrote a story to correspond.
There are some questions concerned with particular stories which turn up periodically from every quarter of the globe. In “The Adventure of the Priory School “Holmes remarks in his offhand way that by looking at a bicycle track on a damp moor one can say which way it was heading. I had so many remonstrances upon this point, varying from pity to anger, that I took out my bicycle and tried. I had imagined that the observations of the way in which the track of the hind wheel overlaid the track of the front one when the machine was not running dead straight would show the direction. I found that my correspondents were right and I was wrong, for this would be the same whichever way the cycle was moving. On the other hand the real solution was much simpler, for on an undulating moor the wheels make a much deeper impression uphill and a more shallow one downhill, so Holmes was justified of his wisdom after all.
Sometimes I have got upon dangerous ground where I have taken risks through my own want of knowledge of the correct atmosphere. I have, for example, never been a racing man, and yet I ventured to write “Silver Blaze,” in which the mystery depends upon the laws of training and racing. The story is all right, and Holmes may have been at the top of his form, but my ignorance cries aloud to heaven. I read an excellent and very damaging criticism of the story in some sporting paper, written clearly by a man who did know, in which he explained the exact penalties which would have come upon every one concerned if they had acted as I described. Half would have been in jail and the other half warned off the turf for ever. However, I have never been nervous about details, and one must be masterful sometimes. When an alarmed Editor wrote to me once: “There is no second line of rails at that point,” I answered, “I make one.” On the other hand, there are cases where accuracy is essential.
I do not wish to be ungrateful to Holmes, who has been a good friend to me in many ways. If I have sometimes been inclined to weary of him it is because his character admits of no light or shade. He is a calculating machine, and anything you add to that simply weakens the effect. Thus the variety of the stories must depend upon the romance and compact handling of the plots. I would say a word for Watson also, who in the course of seven volumes never shows one gleam of humour or makes one single joke. To make a real character one must sacrifice everything to consistency and remember Goldsmith’s criticism of Johnson that “he would make the little fishes talk like whales.”
I do not think that I ever realised what a living actual personality Holmes had become to the more guileless readers, until I heard of the very pleasing story of the char-à-banc of French schoolboys who, when asked what they wanted to see first in [[settings/london|London]], replied unanimously that they wanted to see Mr. Holmes’ lodgings in Baker Street. Many have asked me which house it is, but that is a point which for excellent reasons I will not decide.
There are certain Sherlock Holmes stories, apocryphal I need not say, which go round and round the press and turn up at fixed intervals with the regularity of a comet.
One is the story of the cabman who is supposed to have taken me to an hotel in Paris. “Dr. Doyle,” he cried, gazing at me fixedly, “I perceive from your appearance that you have been recently at Constantinople. I have reason to think also that you have been at Buda, and I perceive some indication that you were not far from Milan.”
“Wonderful. Five francs for the secret of how you did it?”
“I looked at the labels pasted on your trunk,” said the astute cabby.
Another perennial is of the woman who is said to have consulted Sherlock. “I am greatly puzzled, sir. In one week I have lost a motor horn, a brush, a box of golf balls, a dictionary and a bootjack. Can you explain it?”
“Nothing simpler, madame,” said Sherlock. “It is clear that your neighbour keeps a goat.”
There was a third about how Sherlock entered heaven, and by virtue of his power of observation at once greeted Adam, but the point is perhaps too anatomical for further discussion.
I suppose that every author receives a good many curious letters. Certainly I have done so. Quite a number of these have been from Russia. When they have been in the vernacular I have been compelled to take them as read, but when they have been in English they have been among the most curious in my collection.
There was one young lady who began all her epistles with the words “Good Lord.” Another had a large amount of guile underlying her simplicity. Writing from Warsaw, she stated that she had been bedridden for two years, and that my novels had been her only, etc., etc. So touched was I by this flattering statement that I at once prepared an autographed parcel of them to complete the fair invalid’s collection. By good luck, however, I met a brother author on the same day to whom I recounted the touching incident. With a cynical smile, he drew an identical letter from his pocket.
His novels had also been for two years her only, etc., etc. I do not know how many more the lady had written to; but if, as I imagine, her correspondence had extended to several countries, she must have amassed a rather interesting library.
The young Russian’s habit of addressing me as “Good Lord “had an even stranger parallel at home which links it up with the subject of this article. Shortly after I received a knighthood, I had a bill from a tradesman which was quite correct and businesslike in every detail save that it was made out to Sir Sherlock Holmes. I hope that I can stand a joke as well as my neighbours, but this particular piece of humour seemed rather misapplied and I wrote sharply upon the subject.
In response to my letter there arrived at my hotel a very repentant clerk, who expressed his sorrow at the incident, but kept on repeating the phrase, “I assure you, sir, that it was bona fide.”
“What do you mean by bona fide?” I asked.
“Well, sir,” he replied, “my mates in the shop told me that you had been knighted, and that when a man was knighted he changed his name, and that you had taken that one.”
I need not say that my annoyance vanished, and that I laughed as heartily as his pals were probably doing round the corner.
A few of the problems which have come my way have been very similar to some which I had invented for the exhibition of the reasoning of Mr. Holmes. I might perhaps quote one in which that gentleman’s method of thought was copied with complete success. The case was as follows: A gentleman had disappeared. He had drawn a bank balance of £40 which was known to be on him. It was feared that he had been murdered for the sake of the money. He had last been heard of stopping at a large hotel in [[settings/london|London]], having come from the country that day. In the evening he went to a music-hall performance, came out of it about ten o’clock, returned to his hotel, changed his evening clothes, which were found in his room next day, and disappeared utterly. No one saw him leave the hotel, but a man occupying a neighbouring room declared that he had heard him moving during the night. A week had elapsed at the time that I was consulted, but the police had discovered nothing. Where was the man?
These were the whole of the facts as communicated to me by his relatives in the country. Endeavouring to see the matter through the eyes of Mr. Holmes, I answered by return mail that he was evidently either in Glasgow or in [[settings/edinburgh|Edinburgh]]. It proved later that he had, as a fact, gone to [[settings/edinburgh|Edinburgh]], though in the week that had passed he had moved to another part of Scotland.
There I should leave the matter, for, as Dr. Watson has often shown, a solution explained is a mystery spoiled. At this stage the reader can lay down the book and show how simple it all is by working out the problem for himself. He has all the data which were ever given to me. For the sake of those, however, who have no turn for such conundrums, I will try to indicate the links which make the chain. The one advantage which I possessed was that I was familiar with the routine of London hotels — though I fancy it differs little from that of hotels elsewhere.
The first thing was to look at the facts and separate what was certain from what was conjecture. It was all certain except the statement of the person who heard the missing man in the night. How could he tell such a sound from any other sound in a large hotel? That point could be disregarded, if it traversed the general conclusions.
The first clear deduction was that the man had meant to disappear. Why else should he draw all his money? He had got out of the hotel during the night. But there is a night porter in all hotels, and it is impossible to get out without his knowledge when the door is once shut. The door is shut after the theatre-goers return — say at twelve o’clock. Therefore, the man left the hotel before twelve o’clock. He had come from the music-hall at ten, had changed his clothes, and had departed with his bag. No one had seen him do so. The inference is that he had done it at the moment when the hall was full of the returning guests, which is from eleven to eleven-thirty. After that hour, even if the door were still open, there are few people coming and going so that he with his bag would certainly have been seen.
Having got so far upon firm ground, we now ask ourselves why a man who desires to hide himself should go out at such an hour. If he intended to conceal himself in London he need never have gone to the hotel at all. Clearly then he was going to catch a train | which would carry him away. But a man who is deposited by a train in any provincial station during the j night is likely to be noticed, and he might be sure  that when the alarm was raised and his description given, some guard or porter would remember him j Therefore, his destination would be some large town which he would reach as a terminus where all his fellow; passengers would disembark and where he would lose himself in the crowd. When one turns up the time table and sees that the great Scotch expresses bound for [[settings/edinburgh|Edinburgh]] and Glasgow start about midnight, the goal is reached. As for his dress-suit, the fact that he abandoned it proved that he intended to adopt a line of life where there were no social amenities. This deduction also proved to be correct.
I quote such a case in order to show that the general lines of reasoning advocated by Holmes have a real practical application to life. In another case, where a girl had become engaged to a young foreigner who suddenly disappeared, I was able, by a similar process of deduction, to show her very clearly both whither he had gone and how unworthy he was of her affections.
On the other hand, these semi-scientific methods are occasionally laboured and slow as compared with the results of the rough-and-ready, practical man. Lest I should seem to have been throwing bouquets either to myself or to Mr. Holmes, let me state that on the occasion of a burglary of the village inn, within a stone-throw of my house, the village constable, with no theories at all, had seized the culprit while I had got no further than that he was a left-handed man with nails in his boots.
The unusual or dramatic effects which lead to the invocation of Mr. Holmes in fiction are, of course, great aids to him in reaching a conclusion. It is the case where there is nothing to get hold of which is the deadly one. I heard of such a one in America which would certainly have presented a formidable problem. A gentleman of blameless life starting off for a Sunday evening walk with his family, suddenly observed that he had forgotten something. He went back into the house, the door of which was still open, and he left his people waiting for him outside. He never reappeared, and from that day to this there has been no clue as to what befell him. This was certainly one of the strangest cases of which I have ever heard in real life.
Another very singular case came within my own observation. It was sent to me by an eminent London publisher. This gentleman had in his employment a head of department whose name we shall take as Musgrave. He was a hard-working person, with no special feature in his character. Mr. Musgrave died, and several years after his death a letter was received addressed to him, in the care of his employers. It bore the postmark of a tourist resort in the west of Canada, and had the note “Conflfilms” upon the outside of the envelope, with the words “Report Sy” in one corner.
The publishers naturally opened the envelope as they had no note of the dead man’s relatives. Inside were two blank sheets of paper. The letter, I may add, was registered. The publisher, being unable to make anything of this, sent it on to me, and I submitted the blank sheets to every possible chemical and heat test, with no result whatever. Beyond the fact that the writing appeared to be that of a woman there is nothing to add to this account. The matter was, and remains, an insoluble mystery. How the correspondent could have something so secret to say to Mr. Musgrave and yet not be aware that this person had been dead for several years is very hard to understand — or why blank sheets should be so carefully registered through the mail. I may add that I did not trust the sheets to my own chemical tests, but had the best expert advice Without getting any result. Considered as a case it was a failure — and a very tantalising one.
Mr. Sherlock Holmes has always been a fair mark for practical jokers, and I have had numerous bogus cases of various degrees of ingenuity, marked cards, mysterious warnings, cypher messages, and other curious communications. It is astonishing the amount of trouble which some people will take with no object save a mystification. Upon one occasion, as I was entering the hall to take part in an amateur billiard competition, I was handed by the attendant a small packet which had been left for me. Upon opening it I found a piece of ordinary green chalk such as is used in billiards. I was amused by the incident, and I put the chalk into my waistcoat pocket and used it during the game. Afterward, I continued to use it until one day, some months later, as I rubbed the tip of my cue the face of the chalk crumbled in, and I found it was hollow. From the recess thus exposed I drew out a small slip of paper with the words “From Arsene Lupin to Sherlock Holmes.”
Imagine the state of mind of the joker who took such trouble to accomplish such a result.
One of the mysteries submitted to Mr. Holmes was rather upon the psychic plane and therefore beyond his powers. The facts as alleged are most remarkable, though I have no proof of their truth save that the lady wrote earnestly and gave both her name and address. The person, whom we will call Mrs. Seagrave, had been given a curious second-hand ring, snake-shaped, and dull gold. This she took from her finger at night. One night she slept with it on and had a fearsome dream in which she seemed to be pushing off some furious creature which fastened its teeth into her arm. On awakening, the pain in the arm continued, and next day the imprint of a double set of teeth appeared upon the arm, with one tooth of the lower jaw missing. The marks were in the shape of blue-black bruises which had not broken the skin.
